title: Overlap-weighted orthogonal meta-learner for treatment effects over time
one_liner: When you want to predict how a person will respond to medicine at time 5, but almost nobody in your data received that exact sequence of treatments, a weighted system that ignores the rare cases and uses math that doesn't corrupt errors is far more stable.
lead: Imagine you want to predict how a patient will respond to different treatment sequences (a drug for weeks 1 and 2, then a different one for weeks 3-5). The problem: almost nobody has that exact treatment history in your data. As you predict further into the future, the tiny group receiving your treatment sequence shrinks exponentially. Standard methods either ignore this data hunger or become wildly unstable. This paper weights the cases that actually exist in your data and uses a math trick that prevents errors in auxiliary predictions from poisoning the final answer.

problem.h2: Treatment prediction explodes with rare sequences
paras: In medicine, you want to predict what happens if a patient takes a specific sequence of treatments over time. Treatment A weeks 1-2, then treatment B weeks 3-5. The problem is that this exact sequence is rare. Maybe 2% of your data did A for two weeks. Of those, only 30% then did B. Now you are down to 0.6%. Add one more future decision point and you are at 0.2%. Most sequences vanish from your data.

When sequences are rare, standard methods suffer. Some methods (like simple plug-in) ignore the rarity and trust their background predictions, but those predictions are estimated from almost no data, so the errors are huge. Other methods (inverse weighting) reweight the rare cases to correct for scarcity, but they amplify the weight on the tiny population, causing wild swings. Add in the fact that your background predictions (like how often will a patient be given treatment A in the future) are themselves wrong, and that error creeps into every step of your calculation. You get unstable estimates that swing wildly.

callout.html: Focus only on the rare sequences your data actually contains, and use math that blocks errors in the background predictions from poisoning the final answer.

steps.text: Find all treatment sequences that actually appear in your data and their frequencies.
Give higher weight to patients who received sequences that are plausible to observe, ignore the impossible ones.
Train a model to predict future treatments and outcomes (like, given history, what treatment will the doctor choose).
Use a math formula that mixes the data and background predictions in a way that errors in the background cancel out.
Get a prediction that does not swing wildly even when background models are wrong or data is scarce.

paras: The WO-learner changes how you combine three things: the real data from patients, estimates of how often each treatment was chosen (propensity scores), and estimates of what would happen under different treatments (response functions). Instead of treating all data equally or reweighting in a way that amplifies noise, it reweights toward the sequences that are well-supported in the data and uses a math trick that stops errors in the propensity and response estimates from corrupting the final answer.

hidden.h2: The overlap score: which sequences are safe to estimate
hidden.name: Overlap weight for each sequence
paras: The hidden quantity is the overlap score: how plausible is this treatment sequence given what you know about patient history? If a sequence is very rare (low probability), it gets a low score. If it is common (high probability), it gets a high score. The paper estimates this by computing the product of propensity scores along the path (the probability that a patient gets treatment A at step 1, times the probability they get treatment B at step 2, given what happened before, and so on).

Why this matters: when overlap is low for a sequence, the data contains almost no information about what happens under that sequence. Standard methods would reweight that tiny group to correct for rarity, but they are building on sand. The WO-learner instead says: we only make strong predictions for sequences with good overlap. For low-overlap sequences, we hold back and add less noise.

heat.caption: Darker means the treatment sequence has higher overlap (more patients with that path). Bordered cells are sequences where the method makes its strongest predictions.

reads.html: Overlap is how common a treatment path is in your data. Rare paths are shaky to predict. The WO-learner trusts common paths and hedges on rare ones.

Overlap is defined as the product of propensity scores along the treatment sequence. The WO-learner minimizes the overlap-weighted oracle risk, which means it scales its risk by how feasible the sequence is.

mechanism.h2: Why the method stops errors from spreading
paras: The core mechanism is orthogonal learning. In standard causal methods, you estimate propensity (how often is treatment X chosen) and response (what happens under treatment X), then combine them. If your propensity estimate is wrong by 10%, that error multiplies through the rest of the calculation and poisons the final answer. Orthogonal learning is a math construction that isolates the error. You take the difference between the real data and the propensity prediction, weight it by overlap, and mix it with the response prediction in a special way. The math guarantees that small errors in propensity or response do not leak into the final estimate as first-order bias.

The overlap weighting layer adds safety: you only make strong predictions for sequences where your data actually spent time. For rare sequences, the overlap weight shrinks, so you output a more uncertain estimate. This prevents the method from confidently predicting behavior for a treatment sequence that appears once in 10,000 patients. Combined, overlap weighting plus orthogonality means you are stable against two sources of error: (1) wrong background predictions, and (2) trying to estimate from insufficient data.

stages.s: Compute overlap weight for each sequence path
Estimate propensity (treatment likelihood) and response (outcome likelihood)
Build orthogonal combination (data residual plus weighted response)
Treatment effect estimate, stable under model misspecification

math.words: Weighted risk = mean of (overlap weight times (residual data signal plus adjustment for the response model)) squared. Overlap weight is how common the sequence is. Residual data signal is what the patient actually experienced minus what the propensity model predicted. Response adjustment accounts for how much the response model is wrong.
math.equation: Risk_WO = E[w(a) * ((Y - μ(a)) + (π_error / π(a))) * g(X)]^2, where w(a) is overlap weight, π(a) is propensity, μ(a) is response, π_error is propensity residual
symbols: Overlap weight: how common is treatment sequence a in the data
Actual outcome observed in the data
Propensity score: probability of receiving treatment a given history
Representation function that extracts signal from history

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a sequence has overlap weight 0.6 (60% of similar patients got this treatment).
Patient 1 actually got outcome Y=100. The response model predicted μ=95 (residual of +5).
The propensity was π=0.8. If the propensity model made a small error, π_error=0.02.
The overlap weight of 0.6 dampens the signal. For a rare sequence (weight 0.1), the same error would contribute only 0.25^2 = 0.06, so uncertainty in the rare regime does not dominate the loss.

math.note: The orthogonal term (the propensity error divided by the propensity score) is constructed so that small errors in propensity estimates do not grow as they flow through the calculation.

bars.h2: How stability improves under low overlap

charts.title: Standard inverse weighting (no overlap adjustment)
charts.note: Rare sequences get extreme weights to correct for scarcity, causing huge variance. Average performance collapses.

charts.title: WO-learner (overlap-weighted plus orthogonal)
charts.note: Common sequences stay accurate. Rare sequences get hedged (smaller weight means lower prediction confidence) rather than over-corrected. Overall performance is much more stable.

items.html: If the treatment sequence truly has zero probability (the data generating process forbids it), then even this method cannot estimate it. The overlap weight protects you from the estimation problem but cannot overcome impossibility.

items.b: Propensity estimate is very far wrong.
items.html: Orthogonality protects against first-order bias (small errors in the propensity model do not get multiplied across steps), but if your propensity model is fundamentally misspecified (for instance, it assumes linear relationships when they are nonlinear everywhere), the method still works better than plug-in but not perfectly, because the protection only stops small errors from cascading, not large ones.

items.b: Too few samples in the target regime.
items.html: The method reduces variance for low-overlap sequences, but it cannot create data that does not exist. If zero patients ever received your target sequence, overlap weight becomes undefined.

The method works well when the overlap assumption holds (propensities do not collapse to exactly zero), background models are reasonable approximations (even if imperfect), and you have a decent sample size in at least some regions of the data.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simulation where patients arrive over time, receive treatments A or B at each step, and outcomes depend on the treatments and history. Set the data generation so that certain treatment sequences are rare (e.g., always choosing A has only 5% of samples). Generate ground truth outcomes under all possible sequences, then estimate what the WO-learner predicts. Compare to standard inverse weighting and plug-in methods.
demo.metric_eq: Mean absolute error on rare sequences = |Predicted effect for sequence s - True effect for sequence s| averaged over all sequences with low overlap (propensity < 0.15)
demo.closing: The demo should make it impossible to miss: WO-learner predictions for rare sequences do not blow up like inverse weighting does, and they stay close to the truth even when background models have realistic errors.
